title: Chicago's Great Migration Geography - Claim Ledger

grade_definitions.VERIFIED: Directly confirmed in a primary source or convergent independent secondary sources.
grade_definitions.SUPPORTED: Backed by credible secondary source(s) but lacking primary confirmation or exact provenance.
grade_definitions.PROVISIONAL: Single tertiary/popular source or unverified; usable only with qualification.

claims.claim: Chicago's Black population was 44,103 (about 2%) in 1910 and 1,102,620 (32.75%) in 1970.
claims.evidence: Sibling treated these figures as established from decennial Census tables.
claims.contradictory_evidence: No exact Census table/provenance located in new research this round.
claims.notes: Sibling-derived. Downgrade risk: exact table provenance not yet re-verified; target for Census-table check in next round.

claims.claim: Chicago's Black population peaked at 1,187,905 in 1980 and fell to 787,551 by 2020.
claims.evidence: Sibling corpus figures; beyond this brief's 1916-1970 window but frames later reversal.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found.
claims.notes: Sibling-derived; context only.

claims.claim: Hansberry v. Lee (1940) struck down restrictive-covenant enforcement in Chicago, involving a Woodlawn covenant scheme.
claims.evidence: Sibling cites court opinions; new research (Encyc. Chicago; fourteeneast) confirms case facts.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None; caveat: covenants remained common after 1940 and Shelley (1948) was the national blow.
claims.notes: Sibling-derived; corroborated by new research.

claims.claim: The CHA's 1950 segregated siting decision channeled public housing into Black neighborhoods; Gautreaux litigation followed (1966-1976).
claims.evidence: Sibling's strongest housing-policy material; consistent with new findings on the Neighborhood Composition Rule.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.notes: Sibling-derived; reinforces this brief's second-wave claims.

claims.claim: Pullman porters distributed the Chicago Defender across the South.
claims.evidence: Sibling red-team downgraded this to PROVISIONAL: plausible and widely repeated, but primary verification missing.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None direct; IC-train circulation is well documented, porter-specific claims less so.
claims.notes: Sibling-derived; do not upgrade without a primary source.

claims.claim: Contract selling exploited Black homebuyers in second-wave Chicago (esp. North Lawndale); the Contract Buyers League organized resistance from 1968.
claims.evidence: Sibling's strongest material; corroborated by Moyers & Company documentary, Ta-Nehisi Coates's 'The Case for Reparations,' and Beryl Satter's Family Properties.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Clyde Ross purchase year/price conflict (1958/$27,000 vs 1961/$26,000) remains unresolved.
claims.notes: Sibling-derived; corroborated by new research.

claims.claim: Roughly 75% of Black Chicagoans lived in the South Side 'Black Belt' through mid-century.
claims.evidence: New research corroborates: talkingblackinamerica.org viewer guide states that by mid-century 75% of the Black population lived in the South Side chain of neighborhoods.
claims.contradictory_evidence: AIC curriculum claims >90% of Black Chicagoans in Bronzeville by the 1930s - definitional tension (Bronzeville boundaries vs. Black Belt census tracts).
claims.notes: Sibling-derived; now corroborated but with definitional caveat.

claims.claim: The Chicago Defender catalyzed migration; causal weight vs. labor demand is debated.
claims.evidence: Consensus that the Defender encouraged migration; sibling red-team keeps causation qualified.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Labor demand and chain migration as competing/co-causes.
claims.notes: Sibling-derived; keep attribution qualified in brief.

claims.claim: About 500,000 Black southerners migrated to Chicago across the Great Migration.
claims.source: Sibling brief CTL-DR-BCI-001 (via Chicago Black Renaissance landmark report)
claims.evidence: Relayed in landmark report and popular summaries; consistent with net population growth 1910-1970 (~1.06M).
claims.contradictory_evidence: No single audited migration-flow table located; net-growth arithmetic is approximate.
claims.notes: Sibling-derived; net-flow figure, not an exact count.

claims.claim: The first migration wave to Chicago ran c. 1916-1930 (50,000+ arrivals 1916-1919); the Depression slowed movement and WWII opened the second wave.
claims.source: Chicago Urban League CULtivate report, Part 1
claims.evidence: CULtivate cites Black Metropolis on wave timing; Encyc. Chicago: Black pop 44,103 (1910) to 109,458 (1920), 148% increase.
claims.contradictory_evidence: No conflict; periodization is conventional.
claims.notes: New. Keeps waves distinct per assignment.

claims.source: CULtivate; Encyc. Chicago; American Immigration Council; sibling
claims.evidence: Values converge across independent secondary sources citing decennial censuses; 1920 figure has a 50-person variant between sources.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Exact Census table numbers not yet located; 1920 variant 109,458 vs 109,408.
claims.notes: New. Per standard: without exact table provenance, no better than SUPPORTED.

claims.claim: First-wave migrants came chiefly from Mississippi, Arkansas, and Alabama, arriving by Illinois Central Railroad at the 12th Street & Michigan Avenue station.
claims.source: American Immigration Council curriculum; Encyc. Chicago demography page
claims.evidence: AIC lesson plan (Smithsonian-linked, 2019) states origin states and station location; Encyc. Chicago corroborates origin states.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.notes: New. Arrival geography anchors settlement analysis.

claims.claim: Early Black settlement in Chicago centered near the Illinois Central station at 12th & Michigan, adjacent to South Side job districts.
claims.evidence: AIC: migrants 'settled nearby' the station; South Side stockyard/factory job access.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.notes: New.

claims.claim: In 1919, most Black Chicagoans lived between the railroad (west), 30th Street (north), 40th Street (south), and Ellis Avenue (east).
claims.source: Walter White, 'Chicago and Its Eight Reasons,' The Crisis, Oct. 1919
claims.evidence: Contemporary eyewitness description by NAACP investigator published weeks after the 1919 riot.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Boundary descriptions vary by author/year (see N-06, N-07); this is a 1919 snapshot.
claims.notes: New. VERIFIED as an accurate record of White's contemporary description.

claims.claim: Through the 1920s the majority of Black residents lived between State Street, 31st Street, Cottage Grove Avenue, and 47th Street.
claims.source: CULtivate report relaying Black Metropolis (Drake & Cayton, 1945)
claims.evidence: CULtivate attributes boundaries to Drake & Cayton's 1945 community study.
claims.contradictory_evidence: White (1919) gives slightly different 1919 bounds; consistent with slight southward shift over the 1920s.
claims.notes: New. Note definitional: 'majority of Black residents' vs 'the Black Belt.'

claims.claim: By the 1940s the Black Belt was commonly bounded by Cermak Road, Lake Michigan, South Chicago Avenue, and LaSalle Street.
claims.evidence: CULtivate census-tract analysis for the 1940s.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Popular summaries give 22nd-63rd/State-Cottage Grove (peak Bronzeville) - different descriptive frame, not contradictory.
claims.notes: New.

claims.claim: 58 racial bombings (housing-related) occurred in Chicago from July 1917 to March 1921.
claims.source: Chicago Commission on Race Relations, The Negro in Chicago (1922); corroborated by Britannica, Chicago Fed WP, ISBA
claims.evidence: Later summaries attribute the 58-bombing count directly to the Commission's 1922 report; count independently corroborated.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Walter White (1919) counted 20+ Jan 1918-Aug 1919 - consistent sub-period, not contradictory.
claims.notes: New. Count treated as VERIFIED via primary attribution; direct page check still advisable.

claims.claim: 32 of those bombs fell within 41st-60th Streets, Cottage Grove to State - the densest Black settlement zone.
claims.source: Chicago Commission on Race Relations via ISBA (2019)
claims.evidence: ISBA quotes the Commission's geographic distribution of the 58 bombings.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.notes: New. Direct Commission page check recommended.

claims.claim: At least 20 bombings outside the Black district, Jan 1918-Aug 1919, produced 2 arrests and 0 convictions.
claims.evidence: White's first-hand 1919 accounting; 'not one conviction' is his contemporary claim.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on counts; enforcement failure corroborated by Commission.
claims.notes: New. VERIFIED as accurate record of White's contemporary reporting.

claims.claim: The 1919 Chicago race riot ran July 27-Aug 3, 1919: 38 killed (23 Black, 15 white), 537 injured, 1,000-2,000 left homeless, most homeless Black.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago; Chicago Reader; Britannica
claims.evidence: Three independent secondary sources converge on dates and casualty figures; triggered by Eugene Williams's drowning at 29th Street beach.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Casualty counts vary slightly across popular sources; 38/23/15 is the encyclopedic consensus.
claims.notes: New. Context for settlement violence; not a settlement claim per se.

claims.claim: In 1919 Rev. Lacy Kirk Williams said 125,000 Black Chicagoans were crowded into quarters formerly accommodating 50,000.
claims.evidence: CULtivate attributes the quote to Williams (Olivet Baptist pastor) speaking in 1919.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Figures are advocacy-era estimates; compare 109,458 in 1920 Census - Williams's 125,000 is plausible for 1919 with undercounting.
claims.notes: New. Quote is evidence of perceived crowding; not a census count.

claims.claim: 62% of 274 Black families sampled in the 1920s took in lodgers to afford rent.
claims.source: Chicago Commission on Race Relations via Journal of Urban History (D. Young, on Edith Abbott's study)
claims.evidence: Peer-reviewed article reports the Commission's 1920s finding of 62% of 274 families renting to lodgers.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.notes: New. VERIFIED as accurate relay; original Commission table check advised for table number.

claims.claim: Black families carried a heavier rent burden: 80.7% of white families spent <20% of income on rent, while >80% of Black families spent >23%.
claims.source: Helen Houghteling study via Young, Journal of Urban History
claims.evidence: Single-study finding relayed in peer-reviewed article.
claims.contradictory_evidence: No independent corroboration located this round.
claims.notes: New. Keep as study-specific finding, not citywide census fact.

claims.claim: A September 1923 Chicago Defender notice described 2-4 married couples crowded into single 7-8 bedroom apartments.
claims.source: Chicago Defender via Young, Journal of Urban History
claims.evidence: Peer-reviewed relay of a specific Defender housing notice.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.notes: New. Illustrative of first-wave overcrowding.

claims.claim: Olivet Baptist Church, under Rev. Lacy Kirk Williams (pastor from 1916), directed migrants to housing, provided childcare and the city's first kindergarten, and became a national model of migrant ministry.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago (Wallace Best); WBEZ (2026); Preservation Chicago
claims.evidence: Encyc. Chicago entry by scholar Wallace Best; 2026 WBEZ profile; Preservation Chicago history. Congregation bought the 3101 S. King Drive building in 1918.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on the core claim; 'first kindergarten in the city' is Best's characterization.
claims.notes: New. Key enabler: reception infrastructure for first-wave arrivals.

claims.claim: The Wabash Avenue YMCA (3763 S. Wabash) provided lodging, job training, and education to newly arrived migrants; opened 1913 per NPS, 1914 per Wikipedia; the ASNLH was founded there in 1915.
claims.source: NPS National Register nomination; Wikipedia (Wabash YMCA); AIC
claims.evidence: NPS nomination (federal, primary-grade) confirms Rosenwald-funded YMCA and migrant services; opening-year variant 1913 vs 1914.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Opening year 1913 (NPS) vs 1914 (Wikipedia); function claims converge.
claims.notes: New. Second institutional enabler of first-wave settlement.

claims.claim: The Chicago Defender encouraged migration through front-page articles, success stories, and notices, and circulated in the South via Illinois Central trains.
claims.evidence: CULtivate documents Defender's migration coverage and rail distribution.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Causal weight vs. labor demand debated (see S-08).
claims.notes: New. Enabler of arrival; not sole cause.

claims.claim: Chain migration: migrant families pooled money to buy a single train ticket, sending one member ahead.
claims.evidence: AIC lesson plan based on migrant letters and Urban League case files.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.notes: New. Arrival mechanism shaping first-address patterns.

claims.claim: Kitchenette conversions and rooming houses concentrated along Federal and Dearborn Streets: mansions and apartments subdivided, 3-5 families per unit - enabling emergency shelter while deepening exploitation.
claims.source: City of Chicago Black Renaissance landmark report (2020)
claims.evidence: City report documents rooming-house geography and kitchenette subdivision as both emergency housing and exploitative tenure.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None; dual character (enabler + constraint) is the analytical point.
claims.notes: New. Central to this brief's settlement definition (tenure form).

claims.claim: Richard Wright's Native Son (1940) was set in the Black Belt; his 12 Million Black Voices (1941) documented kitchenette life.
claims.evidence: UChicago's Wright biography; dissertation chapter on kitchenettes cites 12 Million Black Voices.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.notes: New. Cultural evidence of settlement conditions, not a settlement statistic.

claims.claim: The Rosenwald Michigan Boulevard Garden Apartments (4618 S. Michigan), built 1929 at ~$3M, were among the first large-scale improved-housing investments for Black Chicagoans.
claims.source: City of Chicago Black Renaissance landmark report
claims.evidence: City landmark report: Julius Rosenwald financed; addressed housing shortage and rent burden.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.notes: New. Enabler: rare quality housing stock amid overcrowding.

claims.claim: After Shelley v. Kraemer (1948) made covenants unenforceable, blockbusting tactics accelerated white flight and Black neighborhood expansion; Chicago Daily News (1959) documented panic-peddling in Chatham.
claims.evidence: Fourteeneast reports scholarly framing of Shelley-to-blockbusting transition; HUD documents 1959 Chatham panic-peddling tactics.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Chatham narrative may compress blockbusting's full complexity; keep as illustrative.
claims.notes: New. Constraint-turned-enabler: exclusion's end enabled expansion via predatory turnover.

claims.claim: South Side Black settlement expanded southward across 63rd, then 75th, then beyond 90th Street; West Side expansion was comparable.
claims.source: Facing History & Ourselves oral history ('Goin' to Chicago')
claims.evidence: Oral-history testimony describes the staged southward march of the color line.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Imprecise as a boundary dataset; interpretive account.
claims.notes: New. Direction of second-wave expansion, not exact boundaries.

claims.claim: By 1950 West Side Black concentrations included blocks bounded by 16th St-Roosevelt Rd-Western Ave-State St and Kinzie St-California Ave-Madison St-Ashland Ave.
claims.evidence: CULtivate's 1950 census-map analysis identifies these West Side concentrations.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None; map-attributed.
claims.notes: New. West Side anchor for second-wave geography.

claims.claim: By 1960 Chicago had 14 majority-Black neighborhoods; North Lawndale was over 90% Black.
claims.source: Chicago Agent Magazine relaying UIC CAGIS research
claims.evidence: Single relay of UIC Chicago Area Geographic Information Study data.
claims.contradictory_evidence: No independent corroboration located this round.
claims.notes: New. Quantifies second-wave clustering.

claims.claim: The Trumbull Park Homes riots began when Betty and Donald Howard, a Black family, moved into the previously white CHA project on July 30, 1953; white violence continued for years, with free Black movement only around 1963.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago (D. Bradford Hunt); SAH Archipedia; Arnold Hirsch (1995)
claims.evidence: Encyc. Chicago and SAH converge on dates and facts; Hirsch's 1995 peer-reviewed article is the scholarly anchor.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on core facts.
claims.notes: New. Constraint case: public-housing integration met organized violence.

claims.claim: The CHA's 'Neighborhood Composition Rule' concentrated 1950s-60s public housing (168 high-rise buildings, ~19,700 units) in predominantly Black South Side areas, with some West Side development.
claims.evidence: CULtivate attributes the building/unit counts to its cited source.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Counts need the underlying source check before VERIFIED.
claims.notes: New. Constraint: state-built segregation in the second wave.

claims.claim: Restrictive covenants covered roughly 80% of Chicago's residential property.
claims.evidence: Single tertiary source; sibling flagged this as unsupported.
claims.contradictory_evidence: No primary covenant-coverage study located; '80%' may reflect an often-repeated estimate.
claims.notes: New. Do not use without better sourcing.

claims.claim: HOLC's Chicago residential-security maps formalized racialized notions of lending risk and are associated with later segregation and disinvestment, but were produced after most HOLC lending was complete and did not directly control HOLC lending.
claims.evidence: Fed researchers document map timing vs. lending; effects paper associates maps with later segregation.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Popular accounts often overstate direct HOLC-lending causation.
claims.notes: New. Precision point: FHA underwriting and appraisal systems were the more direct discriminatory mechanisms.

claims.claim: Bronzeville at its peak held 300,000+ residents in a ~7-mile strip (roughly 22nd-63rd, State to Cottage Grove) - described as the 'Black Metropolis.'
claims.evidence: Popular histories converge on scale and boundaries; consistent with census-based figures.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Popular sources; boundary language ('22nd-63rd') is descriptive, not a census definition.
claims.notes: New. Use as descriptive scale, not a statistical claim.

claims.claim: The Black Belt's street fabric ran along State, Federal, Dearborn, Wabash, Michigan, South Park, Grand Boulevard, and Wentworth.
claims.evidence: Curriculum material listing the corridor streets of the Black Belt.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.notes: New. Settlement morphology detail.

claims.claim: Park Manor's first Black family and Chatham pioneers (e.g., Joe LaRue moving to Chatham in 1960) mark the second wave's far-South-Side expansion.
claims.evidence: Oral testimony and Newcity profile document individual pioneer moves.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Individual cases; not neighborhood-level statistics.
claims.notes: New. Micro-level settlement evidence.

claims.claim: The Chicago Commission on Race Relations' 672-page report The Negro in Chicago (1922, University of Chicago Press) documented the 58 bombings, housing conditions, and riot causes; a full scan is publicly available via Internet Archive (NYPL copy).
claims.source: Internet Archive metadata (verified 2026-09-28) + report contents via secondary summaries
claims.evidence: IA metadata verified: creator Chicago Commission on Race Relations, 1922, U. Chicago Press, 832 scanned pages, copyright status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT (US).
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.notes: New. Primary-source artifact; title page downloaded into visuals/.

claims.claim: Wilson & Co.'s 1955 packinghouse closure hit 2,000+ Black workers, undercutting the industrial job base that had anchored second-wave settlement near the stockyards.
claims.evidence: DePaul labor-history material on packinghouse closure and UPWA.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Single source; employment-settlement linkage is interpretive.
claims.notes: New. Economic enabler/constraint of second-wave settlement.

claims.claim: A 1944 estimate put Chicago's Black population at 337,000.
claims.evidence: Single scholarly relay; consistent with 1940 (277,731) and 1950 (492,265) census figures.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Single-sourced; no census for 1944.
claims.notes: New. Intercensal estimate; keep qualified.

claims.claim: Ida B. Wells Homes were designated for Black families; Altgeld Gardens was an early Black-occupied CHA development.
claims.evidence: CULtivate names Wells and Altgeld Gardens in its CHA history.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Pre-1950 CHA Black occupancy figures remain a sibling-identified gap.
claims.notes: New.
